## The Story {#the-story .section-divider background-image="images/story-bg.jpg" background-size="cover" background-position="center" background-opacity="0.5"}

<div class="section-number">01</div>

<div class="divider-title">The Story</div>

<div class="divider-subtitle">
  Why Singapore's low fertility is not just a headline about fewer babies, but a long-term demographic shift.
</div>

---

## Birth counts show the drop — but not the reason {.story-slide}

<div class="kicker">Starting point</div>

<div class="story-big">
Singapore's fertility decline is not just about <span>fewer births</span>.
</div>

<div class="story-sub">
The bigger question is what changed beneath the numbers: family timing, marriage patterns, work-life pressures and family size.
</div>

<div class="story-question">
<strong>Key question:</strong> What demographic and social changes are associated with Singapore's persistently low fertility?
</div>

---

## From “how many births?” to “what changed?” {.lens-slide}

<div class="kicker">Our analytical lens</div>

<div class="lens-grid">

<div class="lens-card">
  <div class="lens-num">01</div>
  <strong>Fertility timing</strong>
  <small>Are births shifting from women in their 20s toward women in their 30s?</small>
</div>

<div class="lens-card">
  <div class="lens-num">02</div>
  <strong>Family formation</strong>
  <small>Are marriage and parenthood happening later, reducing time for larger families?</small>
</div>

<div class="lens-card">
  <div class="lens-num">03</div>
  <strong>Family size</strong>
  <small>Even after marriage, are completed family sizes becoming smaller?</small>
</div>

<div class="lens-card">
  <div class="lens-num">04</div>
  <strong>Policy context</strong>
  <small>Did policy shifts coincide with sustained fertility recovery?</small>
</div>

</div>

---

## Original Visualisation & Critique {#original-visualisation .section-divider background-image="images/critique-bg.jpg" background-size="cover" background-position="center" background-opacity="0.5"}

<div class="section-number">02</div>

<div class="divider-title">Original Visualisation & Critique</div>

<div class="divider-subtitle">
  We start from an online news media visualisation, then evaluate what it communicates well and what it leaves unexplained.
</div>

---

## The original CNA visualisation {.clean-slide}

<div class="two-col">

<div class="image-frame">
  <img src="images/cna_birth_chart.png" alt="CNA birth chart">
  <div class="caption">Source: CNA, “Drop in Singapore citizen births in 2022”; National Population and Talent Division.</div>
</div>

<div class="side-note">
  <div class="kicker">What it shows</div>
  <h3>Annual Singapore citizen births, 2012–2022</h3>
  <p>The chart uses vertical bars to compare birth counts across years, with two five-year average annotations to highlight the decline between 2013–2017 and 2018–2022.</p>
  <p><strong>Core message:</strong> citizen births fell to 30.4k in 2022, the lowest value shown in the chart.</p>
</div>

</div>

---

## Strengths: why the chart works {.clean-slide}

<div class="kicker">Visual critique</div>
<h2>Clear, readable and fast to understand</h2>
<div class="hr-accent"></div>

<div class="card-grid-3">

<div class="info-card good">
  <div class="num">01</div>
  <h3>Direct message</h3>
  <p>The title and value labels make the intended takeaway obvious: Singapore citizen births dropped in 2022.</p>
</div>

<div class="info-card good">
  <div class="num">02</div>
  <h3>Simple encoding</h3>
  <p>Vertical bars are easy to compare, especially because every bar has a direct birth-count label.</p>
</div>

<div class="info-card good">
  <div class="num">03</div>
  <h3>Period comparison</h3>
  <p>The two colour groups and average annotations help readers compare two broad periods instead of only individual years.</p>
</div>

</div>

---

## Weaknesses: what the chart cannot explain {.clean-slide}

<div class="kicker">Visual critique</div>
<h2>The chart describes the outcome, not the drivers</h2>
<div class="hr-accent"></div>

<div class="card-grid-3">

<div class="info-card bad">
  <div class="num">01</div>
  <h3>Birth counts only</h3>
  <p>Raw birth counts are affected by population size and age structure, so they do not directly show fertility behaviour.</p>
</div>

<div class="info-card bad">
  <div class="num">02</div>
  <h3>Short time horizon</h3>
  <p>The 2012–2022 range is useful for news reporting but too short for understanding Singapore's long-term fertility transition.</p>
</div>

<div class="info-card bad">
  <div class="num">03</div>
  <h3>No age or context</h3>
  <p>The chart does not show whether births shifted by maternal age, nor how fertility changed alongside policy, singlehood or employment patterns.</p>
</div>

</div>

---

## Raw layout snapshots {.clean-slide}

<div class="kicker">Data structure</div>
<h2>Most sources are wide-format files, but their row structures differ</h2>
<div class="hr-accent"></div>

<table class="custom-table">
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>Dataset</th>
      <th>Raw layout</th>
      <th>Main cleaning need</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Births & fertility</td>
      <td>Single-block wide table: data series in rows, years 2025 → 1960 in columns</td>
      <td>Filter ASFR/TFR rows and reshape year columns to long format</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Singlehood</td>
      <td>Metadata rows + hierarchical age group / male / female rows</td>
      <td>Remove metadata, fill age groups, keep female rows, reshape to long</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Female LFPR</td>
      <td>Total, male and female blocks with detailed and aggregate age rows</td>
      <td>Extract female resident participation rows and selected age groups</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Policy / recession</td>
      <td>Manual annotation tables</td>
      <td>Keep separate from numerical datasets for labels and shading only</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

## Data Engineering Workflow {#engineering-workflow .section-divider background-image="images/workflow-bg.jpg" background-size="cover" background-position="center" background-opacity="0.5"}

<div class="section-number">05</div>

<div class="divider-title">Data Engineering Workflow</div>

<div class="divider-subtitle">
  The pipeline standardises multiple raw layouts into consistent, analysis-ready tables while preserving missing-value meaning and source traceability.
</div>

---

## Raw → clean → analysis-ready {.clean-slide}

<div class="kicker">Pipeline overview</div>
<h2>One reproducible workflow for all datasets</h2>
<div class="hr-accent"></div>

<div class="pipeline">

<div class="pipe-step">
  <div class="step-id">STEP 01</div>
  <h3>Import</h3>
  <p>Read raw CSV files and identify where the true table header begins.</p>
</div>

<div class="pipe-step">
  <div class="step-id">STEP 02</div>
  <h3>Clean</h3>
  <p>Remove metadata rows, standardise labels and convert values to numeric.</p>
</div>

<div class="pipe-step">
  <div class="step-id">STEP 03</div>
  <h3>Reshape</h3>
  <p>Convert year columns into long format using a consistent year variable.</p>
</div>

<div class="pipe-step">
  <div class="step-id">STEP 04</div>
  <h3>Derive</h3>
  <p>Calculate indicators such as mean singlehood, mean LFPR and fertility timing metrics.</p>
</div>

<div class="pipe-step">
  <div class="step-id">STEP 05</div>
  <h3>Validate</h3>
  <p>Check expected year ranges, age groups and reconstructed TFR values.</p>
</div>

</div>

---

## Cleaning decisions {.clean-slide}

<div class="kicker">Transformation choices</div>
<h2>Key decisions that protect interpretability</h2>
<div class="hr-accent"></div>

<table class="custom-table">
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>Issue</th>
      <th>Decision</th>
      <th>Why it matters</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Years stored as columns</td>
      <td>Use long format with one row per year-variable observation</td>
      <td>Required for joining, plotting and time-series analysis</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Different coverage periods</td>
      <td>Preserve unavailable values as <code>NA</code></td>
      <td>Missing data is not the same as zero</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Different units</td>
      <td>Keep ASFR, TFR and percentages as separate measures</td>
      <td>Prevents misleading dual-axis interpretation</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Annotation events</td>
      <td>Store policy and recession periods in separate lookup tables</td>
      <td>Avoids duplicating contextual events into every yearly row</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

---

## Target output schema {.clean-slide}

<div class="kicker">Final data structure</div>
<h2>Cleaned tables prepared for visualisation and analysis</h2>
<div class="hr-accent"></div>

<div class="schema-grid">

<div class="schema-card">
  <h3><code>fertility_by_age</code></h3>
  <p>One row per year × maternal age group, containing ASFR and derived TFR contribution.</p>
</div>

<div class="schema-card">
  <h3><code>annual_context</code></h3>
  <p>One row per year, containing TFR, mean female singlehood and mean female LFPR indicators.</p>
</div>

<div class="schema-card">
  <h3><code>family_size_40_49</code></h3>
  <p>Family-size distribution among ever-married resident females aged 40–49.</p>
</div>

<div class="schema-card">
  <h3><code>policy_annotations</code></h3>
  <p>Selected population policy events and demographic milestones for timeline labels.</p>
</div>

<div class="schema-card">
  <h3><code>recession_annotations</code></h3>
  <p>Economic downturn periods for optional contextual shading and interpretation boundaries.</p>
</div>

<div class="schema-card">
  <h3><code>survey_reasons</code></h3>
  <p>Marriage and Parenthood Survey indicators used to support practical-constraint interpretation.</p>
</div>

</div>

## Insight package placeholders {.clean-slide}

<div class="card-grid-3">

<div class="info-card blue">
  <div class="num">INSIGHT 01</div>
  <h3>Later, but not recovered</h3>
  <p>Childbearing moved towards older ages, but later-age gains did not fully offset younger-age losses.</p>
</div>

<div class="info-card blue">
  <div class="num">INSIGHT 02</div>
  <h3>Smaller families after marriage</h3>
  <p>Among ever-married women aged 40–49, larger families became less common over time.</p>
</div>

<div class="info-card blue">
  <div class="num">INSIGHT 03</div>
  <h3>Practical constraints</h3>
  <p>Survey evidence can explain why preferred family size may differ from realised family size.</p>
</div>

</div>

---

## Limitations {.clean-slide}

<div class="kicker">Interpretation boundaries</div>
<h2>What our analysis can and cannot claim</h2>
<div class="hr-accent"></div>

<div class="limit-grid">

<div class="limit-card">
  <h3>Correlation ≠ causation</h3>
  <p>We identify patterns and co-movements, not direct causal effects of any single factor.</p>
</div>

<div class="limit-card">
  <h3>Period measures</h3>
  <p>TFR and ASFR describe fertility in a given year, not the completed experience of one cohort.</p>
</div>

<div class="limit-card">
  <h3>Data comparability</h3>
  <p>Some series use census, survey and administrative sources, so methodology notes must be retained.</p>
</div>

</div>

---

## Conclusion {#conclusion .clean-slide}

<div class="kicker">Final takeaway</div>

<div class="conclusion-big">
Singapore's fertility decline appears to be an <span>entrenched structural issue</span>: policy matters, but delayed family formation and smaller realised family sizes make low fertility harder to reverse.
</div>

<div class="story-question">
Final sentence to refine after plots are finalised: low fertility is not only about fewer births in one year, but about how the pathway into parenthood has changed over decades.
</div>
